frameworks.name: Problem-to-Problem Continuity
frameworks.definition: Products keep customers by positioning the initial problem's solution as creating a new problem that only the product can solve.

frameworks.name: Consumable Deliverables Model
frameworks.definition: A community retention model where customers receive education once (black box system) but must repeatedly purchase consumable inputs (supplies, data, updates) to operate the system.

claims.text: Offers with aggressive promises (e.g., "lose 10 kg in 90 days") convert higher but churn faster, because customers have higher expectations and more reasons to leave once the promise expires. Offers with minimal promises (e.g., "this may or may not work, buy only if you're this type of person") convert slower but have significantly lower churn.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: High promises create high expectations and high exit criteria; low promises create lower expectations and lower reasons to leave
bounded_by: The claim assumes the buyer can assess whether they are the 'right type of person'

claims.text: Community retention depends on whether members stay for the founder's ongoing value creation or because other community members create value for each other. If members depend on the founder, the founder must continuously generate new content; if members depend on each other, retention occurs naturally without ongoing founder input.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to broadcast communities where founder value is the primary retention driver

claims.text: When the first problem in a system is solved, it creates a second problem. Retention increases when the product clearly frames what that new problem is, making the customer's need for the product continuous rather than one-time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Problem continuity creates persistent customer need because solving problem A reveals problem B that only the original system can address

claims.text: The best low-churn community model combines education (teaching customers a system one time) with ongoing consumable deliverables (supplies, data, or updates the customer must buy to operate the system). Low-churn founder-driven communities segment into two parts: black-box system (education) and consumable inputs (news/supplies).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to peer-to-peer communities where value flows between members, not from founder

claims.text: A 3D printing community achieved approximately 2-3% monthly churn by scraping and providing weekly updates on top-ranked products selling in the category, after teaching members the core skill. Members stayed not for the education (received once) but for the weekly consumable news about which products were currently performing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder scrapes and curates external data
bounded_by: Requires ability to continuously scrape and curate relevant external information in the niche

claims.text: A wholesale real estate community sustained retention by combining the initial system (how to find and flip wholesale properties) with a weekly consumable deliverable (hot list of new property addresses updated weekly). Members needed to repurchase the address list each week to operate the original system they learned.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Requires access to curated, time-sensitive lead data

claims.text: High-qualification communities (screening members heavily upfront) do not necessarily achieve lower churn; high-delivery communities (providing continuous valuable consumables) achieve lower churn regardless of whether qualifications are strict.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: A weight-loss community offered a system (diet and exercise framework) to help members lose weight. After teaching the system in the course, the retention mechanism was: members needed to buy updated supplements, meal plans, or fitness content regularly to operate the system they learned. Without the ongoing consumables, they could not execute the original system.

A real estate wholesale community provided a system teaching members how to identify and flip wholesale properties. Retention came from members repurchasing a weekly-updated 'hot list' of newly available property addresses in their market. The system was one-time education; the consumable was the weekly lead list.

A 3D printing community taught members the core skill of 3D printing design and operation once. The community founder and team scraped the web weekly to identify which 3D-printed products were currently top sellers in marketplaces. Members stayed to access these weekly ranked product lists, which gave them real-time market data to inform their own production and sales decisions.

practices.text: When designing a community offer, minimize the upfront promise to reduce churn; let product quality and fit speak for themselves.
Segment your community value into two parts: one-time education (black box system) and ongoing consumables (news, supplies, updates) to achieve lower churn.
Identify the natural second problem that solving the first problem creates, and ensure your community frames the solution to that second problem.
Set up automated scraping or curation of timely information relevant to your community niche and distribute it regularly to maintain engagement.
